title: SEBI Brings Back Open-Market Share Buybacks: What It Means for Your Investments
description: India's market regulator, SEBI, has decided to reintroduce open-market share buybacks through stock exchanges. A share buyback is when a company buys its own .

faq.q: What is the main difference between open-market and tender offer buybacks?
faq.a: An open-market buyback involves the company purchasing its shares directly from the stock exchange like any other investor. A tender offer, on the other hand, is a direct offer by the company to its shareholders to buy back shares at a specific price, usually higher than the market price.

faq.q: When do the new rules for open-market buybacks start?
faq.a: The new framework for open-market share buybacks through stock exchanges will be effective from August 1, 2026.

faq.q: Are there any limits on how much a company can buy back?
faq.a: Yes, SEBI regulations and the Companies Act, 2013, impose limits on the maximum amount and percentage of shares a company can buy back, usually linked to its net worth and capital.

faq.q: Does a buyback always make share prices go up?
faq.a: While buybacks can create demand and support share prices, an immediate or guaranteed price increase is not certain. Many market factors influence share prices, and the effect of a buyback can be long-term, mainly through improved earnings per share.

faq.q: Why did SEBI phase out open-market buybacks earlier?
faq.a: SEBI had phased out open-market buybacks a year ago due to concerns about potential misuse and to streamline the process, favouring the tender offer route. The reintroduction follows a revised taxation framework and aims to provide greater flexibility while adding new safeguards.
